doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Reviews and being compared to Byas and Gonsalves
summary: Dealing with critics, Sonny Stitt's advice, and the Scott Yanow comparison.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Have you read any of the things that are written about you?

I can’t help reading them. I have learned, it’s safe to say, not to let the bad things bother me and not to let the good things go to my head. I just kind of try real hard to not pay too much attention to them. Obviously I love it when I get good reviews. But Sonny Stitt, this is one thing he said to me and it really strikes home now, you know when all is said and done, you have to please yourself. And only you know if you’ve done what you set out to do a hundred percent and if you’re true to yourself and all that. You’re the only person. Many, many times I’ve had what I think are really bad nights and the audience has like gone crazy, and the opposite. I’ve had horrible nights — I’ve had great nights and nothing, you could hear crickets in the audience. But you are your own worst critic and the only person that really knows. So the reviewers — I used to get really bothered by bad reviews. And when I did get bad reviews it was always because I play the clarinet and I play older material, it was somebody that was saying that I’m just an imitator or I’m trying to do some retro kind of a thing. And these critics now come up with these weird terms like “neo-bop,” “neo-swing,” what does this stuff mean? Meantime here I am

innocently just playing music that I like. And I don’t think about that stuff at all. In fact I did write to one reviewer because he told me the record that I was influenced by in the review, which I’d never heard before. So I had to point that out to him.
Well someone, I think Scott Yanow, who’s a pretty good writer, he said that your tenor mixes Don Byas and Paul Gonzalves.

Yeah. Well see my first inclination is to bristle and say oh how does he know? But it is a compliment and I appreciate that. And those two people, I take that as a compliment because I love both of them. And I guess I could understand where he’s coming from because they were an influence on me. I love both of them and I love a softer kind of a tenor sound anyway. I’m not a loud player, I just don’t do that. I like Zoot a lot too, Zoot Sims. Lucky Thompson. So that kind of thing, it’s like thanks, but again I’m not going to go back to my room thinking oh great, Don Byas and Paul Gonzalves. Because I never feel comfortable if I just rest in one place. I’m trying to just move on. And I don’t want to put myself in a box like that. I don’t want to say this is what I do.
